guion_largo.texto:
Now you leave the plaza behind and head north.

This walk leads to the north complex. According to the INAH, there you will find a cistern, a hall with a polychrome altar, and a temazcal.

The observatory you are leaving behind is, according to the INAH, in caves beneath the north platform. First they were a quarry, and later an observatory. In other words, this part of the city was carved out on the inside and built up on the outside.

The INAH mentions a cistern north of the plaza, part of the water system. México Desconocido describes it as a rainwater cistern with drainage.

As you walk, think about a simple question: where did a city built on a hill get its water? The answer lies in the works that are barely visible.

A temazcal is a steam bath. According to the INAH guide, the one in the north complex had a ceremonial purpose. Other sources place it in other complexes, and there is still no agreement on its exact location.

There is no need to hurry. The walks are designed to be listened to as you move, without looking at the screen. The next stop tells you more about the water.

texto.pregunta: Myth: The observatory is at the top of the pyramid.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is a cave excavated at the base; the light shaft opens at the top.
